scenario: AITA for reducing my tip to compensate for a drink I didn’t order? (US) | So short story, at a restaurant today for lunch I got an entree and a glass of water (not fancy water mind you, just tap and it didn’t even have ice). My girlfriend got the same entree and a tea. When the cheque came we had been charged the same amount, $10 for the entree and $2 for a “beverage”. When I pointed this out to the waitress she said water was a beverage and I needed to pay for it. My girlfriend thinks it was an asshole move and I think I’m not paying $2 for lukewarm tap water. basically I brought my cheque total to the $12.50 it would have originally been without the water added.

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Ethical Perspective: You’re Punishing the Wrong Person** - The server has **no control** over the restaurant’s pricing (e.g., whether water is charged as a "beverage"). They’re just doing their job. - By leaving a **$0.50 tip**, you’re **punishing the server** for something they didn’t cause. This is **unfair** and could lead to resentment or poor service in the future. - If you wanted to "punish" the restaurant, you could: - **Leave a normal tip** and **complain to the manager** (politely). - **Never return** to that restaurant (but this is extreme for a $2 mistake). - **Tip normally** and **forget about it** (adults do this all the time). --- ### **3. Practical Perspective: The Math Doesn’t Add Up** - You’re **overcomplicating** the situation. The restaurant charged you $2 for water because that’s their policy. **You chose to eat there**, so you accepted their terms. - Your **original tip ($2.50) was already a discount** (standard tip is **15–20%** for $12). By reducing it to $0.50, you’re **not saving money—you’re just being petty**. - **Example:** - **Original bill:** $12 (entrée + tea) → **$1.80–$2.40 tip**. - **Your bill:** $14 (entrée + water + tea) → **$2.10–$2.80 tip**. - **Your tip:** $0.50 (which is **less than the standard tip for $12 alone**). --- ### **4. Your Girlfriend’s Perspective is Correct** - She’s right to call it an **asshole move** because: - It’s **rude** to argue with the server over a $2 charge. - It’s **selfish** to punish the server for a policy you agreed to. - It **undermines the culture of tipping**, which relies on **good faith**. - **Better alternatives:** - **Tip normally ($2.50–$3)** and **forget about it** (adults do this all the time). - **Tip normally** and **leave a note for the manager** (e.g., *"We noticed water was charged as a beverage—could this be adjusted in the future?"*). - **Tip normally** and **never bring it up again** (some people don’t care about $2). --- ### **5. What Would a Reasonable Person Do?** A **mature, polite, and fair** approach would be: 1. **Accept the bill as-is** (you chose this restaurant, so you accept their rules). 2. **Tip 15–20%** (e.g., **$2.10–$2.80**)—this is standard and fair. 3. **If you really dislike the policy**, **complain to the manager** (but not to the server). 4. **Move on**—don’t make it a big deal. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1 (Wrong)** - **Why?** Because: - You **punished the wrong person** (the server, not the restaurant). - You **made a small issue into a big one** (over $2). - You **undermined the culture of tipping**, which is built on **gratitude, not negotiation**. - Your girlfriend is **correct**—this was a **petty and unnecessary** move. --- ### **How to Handle It Next Time (If It Happens Again)** If you **really** want to avoid paying for water: 1. **Ask for it before ordering** (e.g., *"Do you charge for water?"*). 2. **If they say yes, don’t order it** (or order tea instead). 3. **If they charge you anyway, tip normally and complain to the manager** (not the server). But **don’t expect the server to refund you**—they’re not the ones setting the prices. --- ### **TL;DR** You were **wrong** to reduce your tip to "punish" the server. Tipping is about **gratitude**, not **bargaining**. A **$0.50 tip** is **rude, petty, and unfair**—especially when your girlfriend called it out. **Next time, tip normally and move on.**
